name: Marco Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the flow-wrappers at Hartley's Biscuits, at the end of the oven line. The biscuits come out of a tunnel oven sixty metres long, they cool, they get stacked, and my machines wrap them in that plastic sleeve you tear open with your teeth. I set the film, line up the print so the logo's in the middle, and keep the seals right. If the seal's too cold the packet pops open in the shop. Sixteen years now, days mostly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The smell, still, after sixteen years. Chocolate digestive day is the best day. What wears me out is when the film tears every ten minutes and the line's backing up and the supervisor's on the radio. Weekends I coach my son Leo's football team, under-twelves, which is its own kind of shift work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there you go, it was a bit overblown. Some good bits, some nonsense, like most things. I'd say that on the touchline more than at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it'd mean I carry on, which is fine by me. I've used AI a few times, it wrote a better complaint letter to the energy company than I would have, and they actually refunded us. That's about the level I'd expect it to stay at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much. Keep the job, keep about three months saved like we've got now. Gina wants a new kitchen, maybe we'd go for that in a couple of years instead of waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty normal, really. Like the weather forecast said storm and it drizzled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it got you a refund. How much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hundred and forty quid. Gina told everyone at her work. So I'd say it's useful for the boring stuff, the letters and forms. It can't line up a print on a flow-wrapper though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything at Hartley's that would change regardless?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're always trimming. We had five on the packing end ten years ago, now it's three because the stacker went automatic. That's just how it goes in food. Slow, a bit at a time.

S0.say: Well, there you go, it was a bit overblown, some good bits and some nonsense like most things. I'd say that on the touchline more than at work.
S0.think: It'd mean I carry on, which is fine by me. I've used AI for a complaint letter that got us a refund, and that's about the level I'd expect it to stay at.
S0.do: Keeps the job at Hartley's and keeps the three months of savings as they are. Considers bringing forward the new kitchen Gina wants within a couple of years.
S0.feel: Calm and ordinary, like a storm forecast that turned into drizzle.
S0.quote: It can't line up a print on a flow-wrapper though.
S0.fieldNote: Marco is even-tempered and sees AI as useful for paperwork, proven by a refund he's proud of. He notes that automation in food has been trimming jobs slowly for years anyway. He doesn't blame anyone for it; to him it's how the industry works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's two sides. The company needs to stay competitive or we all go, and they also owe the staff some training. I'd say both of those, probably to anyone who'd listen in the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit worried. The wrapping end is exactly the sort of thing that gets a new machine with a camera that lines up its own print. That's my main skill gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hartley's does an engineering short course, six months, for operators who want to move into maintenance. Two of the lads did it last year and both got bumped up. I'd sign up for the next round. I'd also get a bit better with the AI stuff, have it explain the wrapper's error codes. And I'd put a bit more into savings, a hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit like the first day of a new season when you don't know the team yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said two lads did the course. Would you have done it without them going first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, probably not. I like to see it work for someone I know. Once Dean did it and came back on better money, I thought, well, he's no cleverer than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner Gina say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say do it, she's been saying it for years. She works on the front desk at a dentist's, and they've got a computer that books everyone now, so she knows the feeling.

S1.say: There's two sides: the company has to stay competitive or we all go, and it also owes the staff some training. I'd say both to anyone who'd listen in the canteen.
S1.think: The wrapping end is exactly where a new machine with a camera lines up its own print. That's my main skill gone, so I'd be a bit worried.
S1.do: Signs up for Hartley's six-month engineering short course after seeing two colleagues promoted from it. Uses AI to explain wrapper error codes and adds 100 a month to savings.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like the first day of a season with a new team.
S1.quote: Once Dean did it and came back on better money, I thought, well, he's no cleverer than me.
S1.fieldNote: Marco moves once he's seen proof from someone he knows, and Dean's promotion is that proof. He sees both sides, company and workers, without blaming either. His wife Gina has already watched computers change her job, so she pushes him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone, and the government needs to slow it down or catch people. Not anti-progress, just, give people a chance. That's what I'd say at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Hartley's would be one of the first. Biscuits are the same thing a million times. If a robot can do the film changes and the cleaning, I'm done. Even the maintenance course wouldn't save me, because the robots fix themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut the kitchen, obviously, and the new car. Save everything, aim for six months. My brother-in-law Rob does tiling, and I've helped him on Saturdays for cash. I'd do more of that, every Saturday, maybe evenings too, so there's something besides Hartley's. And I'd start looking for any job where you're in people's houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. That proper three in the morning feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does two years give you enough time to build up the tiling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not to replace my wage, no. Rob's busy, but not two-men-full-time busy. It's a cushion, a few hundred a month, not a job. And if robots can tile by 2028, then it's nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gives first in the house budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leo's football boots go from new to second-hand, and the takeaway on match days. Gina's car stays, she needs it for work. The kitchen, I'd have to tell her. She'd understand but she'd be gutted.

S2.say: This is too fast for anyone, and the government needs to slow it down or catch people. I'm not anti-progress, I just want people given a chance.
S2.think: Hartley's would be one of the first, because biscuits are the same thing a million times. If a robot can do the film changes and the cleaning, I'm done, and the maintenance course wouldn't save me.
S2.do: Cancels the kitchen and new car and saves everything towards six months. Works with his brother-in-law Rob tiling every Saturday and some evenings for cash, and looks for jobs in people's homes.
S2.feel: Scared, with the three in the morning feeling.
S2.quote: It's a cushion, a few hundred a month, not a job.
S2.fieldNote: Marco's even-handed public line stays the same, but privately he sees his plant as among the first to go. His backup, tiling with Rob, is honest about its limits. Telling Gina the kitchen is off is the moment that hurts him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so let's use it. Companies should train, government should help, people should plan. Everybody does their bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years makes me think the maintenance course is still worth it. If I'm fixing the new machines, I'm maybe the last one out the door, not the first. That's a few years more wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the engineering course in year one, the minute there's a place. Keep doing Saturdays with Rob, start putting that money aside for a van and tools in case I need to go out on my own. Save, steady, two hundred a month. Probably hold off on the kitchen till year three and then decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the sort of anxious where you know what to do on Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait on the kitchen till year three. What would decide it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether Hartley's has started putting in the new kit. If it's in, no kitchen. If they're still talking about it, Gina gets her kitchen. Simple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the under-twelves you coach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing about this, they're eleven. But I'd tell Leo to keep his options open. He wants to be a footballer anyway, so we're already working on plan B.

S3.say: Five years is a fair warning, so let's use it. Companies should train, government should help, people should plan, and everybody does their bit.
S3.think: Five years makes the maintenance course still worth it. If I'm fixing the new machines, I'm maybe the last one out the door, not the first, and that's a few more years of wages.
S3.do: Takes the engineering course in year one and keeps tiling Saturdays with Rob, putting that money aside for a van and tools. Saves 200 a month and holds the kitchen decision until year three.
S3.feel: Anxious, but the kind where he knows what to do on Monday.
S3.quote: If I'm fixing the new machines, I'm maybe the last one out the door, not the first.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Marco becomes methodical: course, side work, savings, and a clear rule for the kitchen. He thinks of the course as buying time, not as a future. His public line stays balanced across every picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no one should be caught out. I'd tell the other dads at football to get their kids into something that needs a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years I can work with. I'd be fifty-three. I think I'd leave Hartley's before it leaves me and go into tiling and bathrooms with Rob properly. People are fussy about their homes. I think they'd want a person in their bathroom longer than in a factory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do the course anyway for the money in the first few years. Keep saving. Around year four, buy the van and tools, go in with Rob as a proper business, two of us. Gina does the books, she's good at that. I'd still keep an eye out, because if robots tile bathrooms by year eight, I'd need a plan C.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. A bit excited about working with Rob, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people are fussy about their homes. Is that a hope or something you've seen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something I've seen. A woman last month made Rob redo a whole row because the grout was a shade too grey. You try programming a robot for Mrs Patel's grout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you about leaving a steady wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quiet months. January, nobody wants a bathroom done. Hartley's pays the same in January as in June. That's why I'd want the savings at six months before I jump.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so no one should be caught out. I'd tell the other dads at football to get their kids into something that needs a person.
S4.think: Ten years I can work with, and I'd leave Hartley's before it leaves me. People are fussy about their homes, and I think they'd want a person in their bathroom longer than in a factory.
S4.do: Takes the course for the extra pay early on and keeps saving towards six months. Around year four buys a van and tools and goes into a bathroom and tiling business with Rob, with Gina doing the books.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly fine, and a bit excited about working with Rob.
S4.quote: You try programming a robot for Mrs Patel's grout.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years turns Marco's Saturday cash work into a real exit plan, and he's quietly pleased about it. He still keeps a plan C in mind for robots that tile. His worry is the January slump, which is why six months of savings is his line before jumping.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. I need time to see things work for other people before I jump, and two years doesn't give me that. What would help is the government paying part of your wage for a year while you retrain or start something, so you're not risking the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the smell. Sounds daft. But I'll miss walking in on chocolate digestive day. Nobody's going to pay me for that, but it's why I've stayed sixteen years.

headlineQuote: I'll miss walking in on chocolate digestive day. Nobody's going to pay me for that, but it's why I've stayed sixteen years.
portrait: Marco Abbott, 43, has run the flow-wrappers at the end of the oven line at Hartley's Biscuits for sixteen years and coaches his son's under-twelves football team at weekends. He's even-handed, always sees two sides, and uses AI now and then for letters and forms. He moves only once he's seen something work for someone he knows, so he joins the maintenance course after a colleague's promotion. AGI in two years alarms him because his backup, tiling with his brother-in-law Rob, is only a cushion, but with ten years he plans to leave Hartley's and build a bathroom business with Rob and his wife Gina.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because he needs time to see things work for others before he jumps, and two years doesn't give him that.
whatWouldHelp: The government paying part of his wage for a year while he retrains or starts something, so the mortgage isn't at risk.
